stem: A client with long-standing diabetes reports gradually progressive burning, tingling, and numbness in both feet. Examination shows reduced vibration and protective sensation bilaterally. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: The pattern is consistent with distal symmetric diabetic peripheral neuropathy and increases risk for unrecognized foot injury.
options.B: The findings indicate an acute unilateral nerve compression because diabetic neuropathy is usually focal and one-sided.
options.C: The loss of sensation shows that glycemic control has improved and no further foot-risk assessment is needed.
options.D: The symptoms are an expected benign effect of aging and are unrelated to diabetes when both feet are involved.

rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care describe distal symmetric polyneuropathy as a common diabetic neuropathy. Small-fiber involvement can cause burning, pain, and tingling, while large-fiber involvement can cause numbness, impaired vibration, and loss of protective sensation. Loss of protective sensation predisposes to unrecognized minor trauma and diabetic foot ulceration. B is inconsistent with the bilateral distal pattern. C and D incorrectly minimize a clinically important diabetes complication.
educational_objective: Recognize distal symmetric diabetic peripheral neuropathy from bilateral distal sensory symptoms and loss of protective sensation, and connect this finding with increased risk for unnoticed foot injury and ulceration.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
source_document_title: Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_locator: Neuropathy section; Recommendations 12.17–12.18; ‘Diagnosis — Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy’ — burning/tingling from small-fiber involvement, numbness and loss of protective sensation from large-fiber involvement; LOPS predisposes to unrecognized minor trauma and diabetic foot ulceration
source_claim_supported: Bilateral distal burning, tingling, numbness, reduced vibration, and loss of protective sensation are compatible with diabetic distal symmetric polyneuropathy and confer increased risk for unrecognized foot injury.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation; identify pathophysiology and manifestations of chronic complications and recognize associated risks
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — diabetic distal symmetric peripheral neuropathy
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source item to replace weak distractors and avoid an oversimplified claim that neuropathy results solely from chronic hyperglycemia. The final item uses the current ADA sensory pattern and loss-of-protective-sensation findings and ties them to clinically important foot-injury risk.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: diabetic peripheral neuropathy / loss of protective sensation
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 12. The symptom and examination pattern is directly supported and the source links LOPS to unrecognized trauma/ulcer risk.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A accurately interprets the bilateral distal sensory pattern without claiming diabetes is the only possible cause of neuropathy in all patients. The stem’s known diabetes and characteristic findings make A the best answer while preserving the general principle that neuropathy is a diagnosis of exclusion clinically.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; the pattern is classic for distal symmetric DPN and LOPS increases foot risk.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; acute focal compression does not best fit a gradual bilateral distal pattern.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; sensory loss is a complication/risk finding, not evidence of improved control.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; bilateral sensory loss should not be dismissed as benign aging in this context.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A integrates the known diabetes, distribution, sensory modalities, and foot-risk implication.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices are clinical interpretations of the same sensory findings.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation is appropriate because the construct is recognition of a chronic neurologic complication and its physiologic consequences.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked DPN as diagnosis of exclusion, small-versus-large fiber manifestations, stocking distribution, hand involvement omission, monofilament interpretation, foot-risk linkage, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
